course.title: Cloud Practitioner Essentials
course.description: A plain-language foundation in how the AWS Cloud works — value proposition, core service categories, global infrastructure, security and IAM, pricing, and the Well-Architected pillars. Content is original and organized around the publicly published AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner domains, so it targets Cloud-Practitioner-style foundations without reproducing any exam material.

questions.prompt: The AWS Cloud is best described as…
options: on-demand IT resources delivered over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing
a single data center in the United States
questions.explanation: Cloud computing is on-demand access to IT resources over the internet, billed for what you use — covered in 'The value of the cloud'.

questions.prompt: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, AWS is responsible for…
questions.explanation: AWS secures the infrastructure; you secure what you put in it — see 'The shared responsibility model'.

questions.prompt: Which service category does Amazon EC2 belong to?
questions.explanation: EC2 provides virtual servers, so it is a compute service — see 'Core service categories'.

questions.prompt: Amazon S3 is primarily a … service.
questions.explanation: S3 stores objects (files) in buckets — see 'Core service categories'.

questions.prompt: An AWS Region is made up of multiple…
questions.explanation: Each Region contains several isolated Availability Zones — see 'Global infrastructure'.

questions.prompt: Which practice best follows the principle of least privilege?
options: sharing the root user login with the team
granting only the permissions a task requires
questions.explanation: Least privilege means the minimum permissions needed — see 'Security and IAM basics'.

questions.prompt: AWS pricing is fundamentally based on…
options: a fixed yearly license per company
paying only for the resources you actually consume
the number of employees you have
questions.explanation: The core model is pay-as-you-go — see 'Pricing and cost management'.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the AWS Well-Architected Framework pillars?
questions.explanation: Cost Optimization is one of the six pillars — introduced in the readings and used in the final project.

lessons.title: Why the cloud, and who secures what
lessons.grammar_note: Two phrases to keep all course: 'in the cloud' = your stuff (you secure); 'of the cloud' = the platform (AWS secures).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the value proposition of cloud computing and state, for any given item, who is responsible for its security under AWS's shared responsibility model. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, name one thing *you* are responsible for and one thing *AWS* is responsible for.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The cloud replaces buying and running your own hardware with renting IT resources on demand over the internet. The value shows up as six benefits worth memorizing: (1) trade large up-front capital expense for variable operating expense, (2) benefit from massive economies of scale, (3) stop guessing capacity, (4) increase speed and agility, (5) stop spending money running data centers, and (6) go global in minutes. Because AWS runs the physical platform and you run what you build on it, security is *shared*: AWS handles security *of* the cloud (hardware, the global network, the facilities, the virtualization layer), while you handle security *in* the cloud (your data, who can access it, encryption settings, operating-system patches on the servers you rent, and your application code).

sections.heading: A concrete example
sections.text: You launch a virtual server (Amazon EC2) to host a website. AWS guarantees the data center has power, cooling, and physical security, and that the hypervisor is patched — that is 'of the cloud'. But if you leave the server's login open to the whole internet, forget to install a security update on its operating system, or store customer data with no encryption, those are your failures, not AWS's — that is 'in the cloud'. The line moves depending on the service: with a fully managed service the customer's share shrinks, but responsibility for data and access is always yours.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Say who is responsible — AWS or the customer: (1) replacing a failed physical hard drive in a data center; (2) choosing a strong password and enabling multi-factor authentication; (3) patching the operating system on a virtual server you launched; (4) physically guarding the building; (5) deciding which users may read a storage bucket. Answers: (1) AWS, (2) customer, (3) customer, (4) AWS, (5) customer.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming 'the cloud is automatically secure', when configuration and access are your job. Mistake: thinking capital expense and operating expense are the same trade-off — the cloud deliberately shifts you from up-front buying to pay-as-you-go. Exit: (a) In one word, does the customer secure things 'in' or 'of' the cloud? (b) Name one of the six cloud benefits. Answers: in; e.g. trade capital expense for variable expense (or 'go global in minutes').

lessons.title: Core service categories: compute, storage, database
lessons.grammar_note: Match the shape of the data to the store: files→object, disks→block, tables→database.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Sort common AWS services into the compute, storage, and database categories, and pick the right *kind* of service for a workload. Warm-up: which category do you think a virtual server belongs to?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: AWS offers hundreds of services, but foundations fit into a few categories. *Compute* runs your code: Amazon EC2 (virtual servers you manage), AWS Lambda (run functions with no server to manage — 'serverless'), and container services such as Amazon ECS/EKS with AWS Fargate. *Storage* holds data in different shapes: Amazon S3 for *object* storage (files and media in buckets), Amazon EBS for *block* storage (virtual disks attached to EC2), Amazon EFS for shared *file* storage, and S3 Glacier tiers for cheap long-term archives. *Databases* store structured data: Amazon RDS and Amazon Aurora for *relational* (tables, SQL), Amazon DynamoDB for *NoSQL* key-value at scale, Amazon ElastiCache for in-memory caching, and Amazon Redshift for data-warehouse analytics.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1: A photo-sharing app needs to store user uploads. Photos are discrete files accessed over the web → object storage → Amazon S3. Example 2: That same app runs its checkout logic only a few times an hour and you don't want to keep a server idle → event-driven functions → AWS Lambda. Example 3: The app needs to store customers, orders, and their relationships with strong consistency → a relational database → Amazon RDS (or Aurora). Notice each choice follows from the *shape* and *access pattern* of the workload, not from a click-path.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Name the category (compute / storage / database) and a fitting service: (1) a virtual disk attached to a server; (2) running a small function on each file upload with no server to manage; (3) a high-scale shopping cart needing single-digit-millisecond key lookups; (4) archiving audit logs for seven years at the lowest cost; (5) a fleet of always-on web servers you fully control. Answers: (1) storage — Amazon EBS; (2) compute — AWS Lambda; (3) database — Amazon DynamoDB; (4) storage — S3 Glacier; (5) compute — Amazon EC2.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling Amazon S3 a 'file system' — it is object storage, not a mountable disk (that's EBS/EFS). Mistake: assuming every database must be relational — DynamoDB is NoSQL and shines at scale. Exit: (a) Which storage type attaches to a single EC2 instance like a disk? (b) Which compute service is 'serverless'? Answers: block storage (Amazon EBS); AWS Lambda.

lessons.title: Global infrastructure: Regions and Availability Zones
lessons.grammar_note: Hierarchy: Region → Availability Zones → data centers; edge locations sit closer to users.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how AWS organizes its infrastructure worldwide and explain why spreading a workload across Availability Zones improves reliability. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what does a Region contain?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: AWS groups its infrastructure geographically. A *Region* is a named physical area (for example, a Region in Ireland or in Northern Virginia) that you choose based on where your users are, data-residency and compliance rules, service availability, and cost. Each Region contains multiple *Availability Zones* (AZs) — one or more discrete data centers with independent power, cooling, and networking, placed far enough apart to isolate faults but connected by low-latency links. Separately, *edge locations* form a global content-delivery network (used by Amazon CloudFront) that caches content close to end users to cut latency. Choosing a Region and designing across several AZs are the two most important infrastructure decisions a beginner makes.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1: Most of your users are in Germany and local law requires data to stay in the EU → pick an EU Region. Example 2: You need your web app to survive a single data-center failure → run servers in at least two Availability Zones in the same Region, so if one AZ goes dark the other keeps serving. Example 3: Users worldwide complain a video loads slowly → put it behind a CDN so edge locations serve cached copies nearby. Each decision maps a business need to a level of the hierarchy.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Choose the right level (Region / Availability Zone / edge location): (1) meeting a legal requirement that data never leaves a country; (2) surviving the loss of one data center within a metro area; (3) reducing load time for viewers on another continent; (4) the place where independent power and cooling isolate a fault; (5) the broadest geographic unit you first select. Answers: (1) Region; (2) Availability Zone; (3) edge location; (4) Availability Zone; (5) Region.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking one Availability Zone is enough for high availability — a resilient design spans two or more AZs. Mistake: confusing an edge location (caching for delivery) with a full Region (where you run and store workloads). Exit: (a) How many AZs should a highly available app use, at minimum? (b) What is an edge location mainly for? Answers: at least two; caching content close to users to reduce latency.

questions.prompt: Securing your customer data and deciding who can access it is…
questions.explanation: Data and access are always the customer's share of the shared responsibility model.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of service to category is correct?
questions.explanation: Amazon RDS is a relational database service.

questions.prompt: 'Serverless' functions that run without you managing a server are provided by…
questions.explanation: AWS Lambda runs code without provisioning servers.

questions.prompt: To survive the failure of a single data center, you should spread a workload across multiple…
questions.explanation: Multiple Availability Zones give fault isolation within a Region.

questions.prompt: Object storage for files and media is best served by…
questions.explanation: Amazon S3 is object storage.

questions.prompt: A benefit of the cloud is trading up-front capital expense for…
questions.explanation: The cloud converts capital expense into variable operating expense.

lessons.title: Security and identity: IAM basics
lessons.grammar_note: Users and roles are *who*; policies are *what they may do*; least privilege is the default mindset.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the building blocks of AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and apply the principle of least privilege. Warm-up: which is safer for daily work — the root user, or an IAM user with only the permissions it needs?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: IAM controls *who* can do *what* in your AWS account. The *root user* is the all-powerful account owner created at sign-up; best practice is to lock it down, add multi-factor authentication (MFA), and not use it for everyday tasks. Instead you create *IAM users* for people or applications, gather them into *groups* to manage permissions together, and attach *policies* — JSON documents that allow or deny specific actions on specific resources. *IAM roles* grant temporary permissions that can be assumed by a user, an application, or an AWS service, avoiding long-lived credentials. The guiding rule is *least privilege*: grant only what a task requires, and widen access only when justified. Layered on top are account-wide safeguards such as MFA and, across many accounts, centralized governance.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1: A new analyst needs read-only access to reports. You create an IAM user, place them in a 'Analysts' group whose policy allows only read actions, and enable MFA — not the root user. Example 2: An application on an EC2 server must read from an S3 bucket. Instead of pasting access keys into the code, you attach an IAM *role* to the instance so it gets temporary, automatically rotated credentials. Example 3: A policy grants full administrator rights 'just in case' — that violates least privilege; you scope it down to the two actions actually used.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each: (1) Which identity should you avoid using for daily work? (2) What do you attach to grant temporary permissions to an EC2 application? (3) What JSON document defines allowed or denied actions? (4) What is the safest permission level to start from? (5) What extra sign-in factor should protect the root user? Answers: (1) the root user; (2) an IAM role; (3) a policy; (4) least privilege (minimum needed); (5) multi-factor authentication (MFA).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using the root user for routine administration — reserve it for the few tasks that require it. Mistake: embedding long-lived access keys in code when a role would supply temporary credentials. Exit: (a) Name the principle of granting only needed permissions. (b) Do policies define *who* or *what they can do*? Answers: least privilege; what they can do.

lessons.title: Pricing and cost management
lessons.grammar_note: Two questions to always ask: how am I *charged* (the pricing model) and how do I *watch* the bill (the cost tools)?

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how AWS charges for resources and name the tools that let you estimate and control spending. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what is the fundamental AWS pricing model?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: AWS pricing rests on *pay-as-you-go*: you pay only for what you use, with no long-term commitment required. For steady, predictable workloads you can commit to lower rates through *Reserved Instances* or *Savings Plans* (a promise of usage over 1 or 3 years in exchange for a discount), while *Spot Instances* offer deep discounts for interruption-tolerant work using spare capacity. A *Free Tier* lets you try many services at no cost within limits. To plan and control spend, AWS gives you the *AWS Pricing Calculator* to estimate a design before you build, *AWS Cost Explorer* to visualize and analyze past spending, *AWS Budgets* to set thresholds and get alerts, and *consolidated billing* through AWS Organizations so multiple accounts share one bill and can pool volume discounts.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1: You want a rough monthly figure for a two-server web app before creating anything → use the AWS Pricing Calculator. Example 2: A batch job can restart if interrupted and you want the lowest price → run it on Spot Instances. Example 3: A production database runs 24/7 all year → a Savings Plan or Reserved Instance beats On-Demand pricing. Example 4: You fear a surprise bill → set an AWS Budget alert so you're notified before spending crosses a limit.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Pick the best fit: (1) estimate cost of a design not yet built; (2) get alerted when spend approaches a limit; (3) analyze last quarter's spending trends; (4) cheapest option for interruption-tolerant batch work; (5) discount for a database that runs steadily for three years. Answers: (1) AWS Pricing Calculator; (2) AWS Budgets; (3) AWS Cost Explorer; (4) Spot Instances; (5) Reserved Instance or Savings Plan.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: putting an interruptible batch job on full-price On-Demand when Spot would be far cheaper. Mistake: confusing the *Pricing Calculator* (estimate the future) with *Cost Explorer* (analyze the past). Exit: (a) What is the default AWS pricing model called? (b) Which tool estimates a design before you build it? Answers: pay-as-you-go; the AWS Pricing Calculator.

items.translation: the split where AWS secures the cloud infrastructure and the customer secures what they put in it
items.example: Under the shared responsibility model, patching your server's operating system is your job, not AWS's.

items.translation: one or more isolated data centers within a Region, with independent power and networking
items.example: Running across two Availability Zones lets the app survive one data center failing.

items.translation: an identity that grants temporary permissions and can be assumed by a user, app, or AWS service
items.example: The server used an IAM role to read the bucket instead of storing long-lived keys.

items.translation: granting only the permissions a task actually requires, and no more
items.example: Following least privilege, the analyst got read-only access rather than admin rights.

items.translation: AWS's core pricing model where you pay only for the resources you consume
items.example: With pay-as-you-go, shutting the servers off overnight lowers the bill.

items.translation: AWS's set of design pillars — including Cost Optimization, Reliability, and Security — for building sound cloud workloads
items.example: Reviewing the design against the Well-Architected Framework flagged a single point of failure.

questions.prompt: The all-powerful account owner you should avoid for daily tasks is the…
questions.explanation: The root user should be locked down and reserved for tasks that require it.

questions.prompt: To give an EC2 application temporary credentials to reach S3, you attach a(n)…
questions.explanation: IAM roles supply temporary, rotated credentials instead of hard-coded keys.

questions.prompt: The cheapest option for interruption-tolerant batch work is…
questions.explanation: Spot Instances use spare capacity at a deep discount for interruptible work.

questions.prompt: To estimate the cost of a design before building it, use…
questions.explanation: The Pricing Calculator estimates future costs; Cost Explorer analyzes past spend.

questions.prompt: A JSON document that allows or denies specific actions on resources is a(n)…
questions.explanation: IAM policies define what an identity is permitted to do.

questions.prompt: Which is a pillar of the AWS Well-Architected Framework?
questions.explanation: Cost Optimization is one of the six Well-Architected pillars.

lessons.title: Applied project: architect a simple cloud solution

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Design a simple cloud solution for a small web application — for example, a photo-sharing site or an online store — and estimate its cost model. You will not build anything; you will produce a written architecture and a rough monthly cost picture that a beginner could defend.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) State the app in one sentence and its expected traffic. 2) Choose services by category: a compute option (e.g. Amazon EC2 or AWS Lambda), a storage option (e.g. Amazon S3 for uploads), and a database (e.g. Amazon RDS or DynamoDB) — and justify each from the workload's shape. 3) Place it in a Region and across at least two Availability Zones, and say why. 4) Add two security measures using IAM (e.g. least-privilege policies, an IAM role for the app, MFA on the root user). 5) Estimate the cost model: which pricing choice fits each resource (pay-as-you-go, Savings Plan/Reserved, or Spot), and which tool you'd use to estimate and monitor spend. 6) Note which AWS Well-Architected pillars your design touches.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ Each service choice is justified by the data shape or access pattern, not named at random. ✔ The design spans two or more Availability Zones for reliability. ✔ Security follows least privilege and protects the root user. ✔ Every resource has a stated pricing model and you named a tool to estimate and watch the bill. ✔ You mapped the design to at least two Well-Architected pillars (e.g. Reliability and Cost Optimization). If all five hold, you've reasoned like a cloud practitioner.
